newsitem.title: USA: NY precious metals end mixed, direction lacking.
newsitem.headline: NY precious metals end mixed, direction lacking.

text.p: New York precious metals futures ended mixed, as the complex continued to try to find some support after last week's renewed weakness, traders said.

"Investor demand for gold remains subdued due to low inflationary expectations and bullish sentiment toward equity markets, while prospects for Japanese gold imports remain bleak as the U.S. dollar continues to appreciate against the yen," Smith Barney analyst David Rinehimer said.
"But the seasonal fourth quarter upturn in gold demand should serve to underpin gold prices through the year-end," he said.
COMEX December gold settled unchanged at $384.60 an ounce after trading from $384.90 to $384.40.
Spot gold bullion ended quoted $382.90/383.40 versus the London afternoon fix of $382.90 and the New York close Friday at $382.55/383.05.
COMEX December silver ended up 0.5 cent at $4.930, after trading in a $4.935-4.915 range.

"The drawdown in COMEX silver stocks to their lowest level since the mid-1980s is perceived more as a transfer in inventories, from exchange to non-exchange depositories, rather than as a sign of end-user demand," Rinehimer said.

Last week both silver and gold recovered to two week highs, on fund shortcovering, with daily momentum indicators turning positive, but the longer term downtrend in place for most of the year still looks intact, analyst said.

The latest CFTC Commitment of Traders data for the week ended October 22, released late Friday, showed large speculators in gold still net short 36,015 lots, while they were 2,499 lots net long in silver.
Traders hope the monthly OTC option expiry Tuesday may provide further direction, traders said.
But with gold trapped in a $380-385 range in the past month, implied volatilities had fallen further to around 4.0 pct for at-the-money one month options, traders noted.
NYMEX January platinum ended up $2.20 at $388.40 an ounce, after seeing fresh three year lows Friday, when the price of platinum also dipped below the price of gold.

The world platinum surplus is forecast to rise to around 7.5 tonnes in 1996, from 6.0 tonnes last year, while platinum demand in Japan was forecast to fall to 70 tonnes this year from 72.5 tonnes last year, analysts said.
Japanese demand for precious metals is seen depressed by the strength of the U.S. dollar which hit a 42 month high against the yen Monday.
NYMEX December palladium settled off $0.65 at $117.60.
Demand for palladium from the electronics industry is down, while the Russians, the world's largest producers of palladium, are seen selling into every price bounce, traders said.
The world palladium surplus is estimated at 1.5 million ounces in 1996, CPM Group analyst Jeffrey Christian said.
--Clive Mckeef, New York Commodities 212-859-1641; email: clive.mckeef@reuters.com
